CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Do not add a new tariff or non-tariff salvo beyond the June 1 rate hike already announced on the existing ~$60B U.S. list. Keep Liu He’s channel open and invite Lighthizer/Mnuchin back to Beijing, aiming at a Trump–Xi conversation at the late-June G20, but offer no new legal-rewrite, enforcement, or purchase commitments while List 3 sits at 25% and Huawei is being restricted. Treat the Huawei/ICT order as a national-security track to be studied and offset with domestic substitution, not mirrored impulsively.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high, not existential. On May 10 the U.S. raised List 3 from 10% to 25% on ~$200B, on top of the earlier $50B at 25%, and USTR began a 25% process on the remaining ~$300B of Chinese goods (timeline 2019-05-05/10; Maritime Executive / Econofact 2019-05-13–14). On May 15 Trump signed EO 13873 and Commerce moved to restrict Huawei, with reporting that Huawei and ~70 affiliates were being placed on the Entity List, cutting U.S. parts without a license (timeline 2019-05-15; Reuters/PCMag 2019-05-15). That is the CHN +0.5 anchor: major export exposure plus firm-level targeting of the national 5G champion. It is not +1.0: industrial production was still +5.0% YoY in May, merchandise exports in the window were still rising, and reserves were stable-to-up at ~$3.12T (country_health CHNPRINTO01IXPYM, XTEXVA01CNM667S, TRESEGCNM052N). The yuan did weaken sharply after the breakdown—onshore to about 6.87 on May 15 from the mid-6.73s at the start of May, with offshore prints near 6.90 and talk of a 7 handle (DEXCHUS; Reuters 2019-05-13)—but reserves are not running and PBOC still has room to defend 7. Talks failed over sovereignty, not over a finished bargain: U.S. sources said Liu offered State Council decrees rather than the statutory changes Lighthizer wanted (Reuters 2019-05-10); Trump accused Beijing of renegotiating (timeline 2019-05-05). China already answered the tariff hike on May 13 with higher rates on the existing ~$60B U.S. list effective June 1 (timeline 2019-05-13). Further escalation now would likely accelerate the $300B consumer list and deepen tech decoupling, while unilateral rollback or purchase concessions after a hike-plus-Huawei move would trade core industrial policy for no reliable relief. Action therefore stays at hold/negotiate: keep the June 1 measure, refuse bitter-fruit law changes, and use the still-open Liu channel and G20 window without new commitments.
key_factors: List 3 now 25% on ~$200B plus live USTR process for ~$300B remaining Chinese goods
May 15 ICT executive order and Commerce move to restrict Huawei (Entity List / U.S. parts licenses)
Talks broke over statutory/enforcement demands vs State Council decrees, not over a signed text
June 1 China retaliation on the existing ~$60B U.S. list already announced — limited unused tariff ammunition
Yuan stress toward 6.87–6.90 but reserves ~$3.12T and IP still positive, so not a financial-stability break
Liu He still engaged in Washington May 9–10; G20/Beijing channel remains the least-cost off-ramp

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump tweets negotiations going too slowly and China attempting to renegotiate; orders List 3 raised from 10% to 25% on May 10 and preparation of tariffs on remaining ~$300B.
List 3 tariff rate rises from 10% to 25%.
China announces it will raise retaliatory tariff rates on its ~$60B US-goods list (higher rates phased in; many effective June 1).
Trump signs Executive Order 13873 (securing information/communications technology supply chains). Commerce moves to restrict Huawei.
CNY/USD weakens from ~6.73 on May 1–3 to 6.8742 on May 15 after the talks break.
China reserves excluding gold ~$3.12T in May, slightly higher over the window — no reserve hemorrhage.
China industrial production still +5.0% YoY as of May 2019 (slowed from March but not contracting).
No progress in Washington: Liu argued policy changes via State Council decrees; Lighthizer wanted previously pledged statutory changes.
Commerce adding Huawei and 70 affiliates to the Entity List, requiring a U.S. license to buy American technology.
China raises tariffs on ~$60B of U.S. exports effective June 1; USTR same day proposes 25% on remaining ~$300B of Chinese goods.
